capture.final_message:
Split the conjunction.

- Apply Dirichlet’s theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions to \(q\ge 1\) and \((a,q)=1\). It gives infinitely many primes \(p\equiv a\pmod q\), exactly the required infinite subtype.

- For the analytic part, use the classical zero-free region
  \[
  \zeta(s)\ne0\qquad\text{when}\qquad
  \Re s\ge 1-\frac{c}{\log |\Im s|},\quad |\Im s|>3.
  \]
  Choose \(A>0\), \(A\le \tfrac12\), sufficiently small so that
  \(1-A/(\log|t|)^9\) lies safely inside this region. The partial-fraction/Hadamard representation for \(\zeta'/\zeta\), together with standard local zero-counting estimates, then gives a uniform bound in the remaining strip near \(\Re s=1\); the much weaker target \(O((\log|t|)^9)\) readily absorbs the usual logarithmic losses. For \(\sigma\) farther to the right, use the absolutely convergent Dirichlet series for \(-\zeta'/\zeta\).

Thus one obtains a single \(C>0\), independent of \(\sigma,t\), after enlarging it to cover the bounded transition range. The essential input is the zero-free region: without it, \(\zeta'/\zeta\) has poles at zeros of \(\zeta\).
